en.instructions: Attach one end of resistance band to wall/upright/... at shoulder height. Insert arm into the loop, at the tricep. Step back until band is pulled straight. Pull back elbow and shoulder against the resistance of the band.

en.name: Incline DB Y-Raise
en.instructions:
1. Set
an incline bench to a 45-degree angle and sit facing the bench, chest
against the pad, with a dumbbell in each hand, palms facing each other.
2. Position your feet firmly on the ground for stability and let your arms hang down naturally with a slight bend in your elbows.
3. Engage your core and keep your back straight throughout the movement.
4. Raise your arms forward and out to form a Y shape, keeping the movement controlled and your elbows slightly bent.
5. Lift until your arms are roughly parallel to the floor and in line with your ears.
6. Pause
briefly at the top of the movement to engage your shoulder muscles
fully, then slowly lower your arms back down to the starting position.
7. Ensure
the movement is slow and controlled during both the ascent and descent
to maximize engagement of the deltoids and supporting muscles.
8. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, maintaining proper form throughout.

en.name: DB Wrist Extension
en.instructions:
: Grab two dumbbells with an overhand grip and lay your forearms across your knees.

: Let your wrists flex fully, then extend your wrists.

en.name: High-Cable Lateral Raise
en.instructions:
Stand next to a cable machine with the pulley set to waist height.

Grab the opposite-side handle with the hand farthest from the
pulley, keeping your palm facing in.

Keep your core engaged, chest lifted, and shoulders relaxed. Maintain a slight bend in the elbow throughout the lift.

Lift your arm out to the side until your elbow reaches shoulder height, keeping your wrist aligned with your elbow.

Briefly pause at the top, then slowly lower the handle back to your side with control. Repeat for the desired reps.

en.name: Shinbox IR Stretch
en.instructions:
Starting Position:Sit on the floor with both hips and knees bent at 90-degree angles.
*Leg Placement:
Place one leg in front of you (external rotation) and the other leg out
to the side/behind you (internal rotation). The shins and knees should
remain flat on the ground.
*The Movement:
Keeping your hips square, hinge your torso forward or tilt it laterally
(side-to-side) toward the front leg to deepen the stretch.
*Target Areas:
Stretches the glutes and piriformis (front leg) and the hip flexors and
quads (back leg). Engages the core and obliques during lateral flexion.
*Goal:* Improves hip mobility, specifically internal and external rotation, and relieves lower back tension.

it.name: Shinbox IR stretch
it.instructions:
Posizione di partenza:Seduti a terra con entrambe le anche e le ginocchia piegate a 90 gradi.
*Posizione delle gambe:
Una gamba è posizionata davanti (rotazione esterna), l'altra è
posizionata di lato/dietro (rotazione interna). Tibie e ginocchia devono
rimanere appoggiate a terra.
*Il movimento:
Mantenendo il bacino dritto, inclinare il busto in avanti o
lateralmente (da un lato all'altro) verso la gamba anteriore per
intensificare l'allungamento.
*Aree coinvolte:
Allunga i glutei e il piriforme (gamba anteriore) e i flessori
dell'anca e i quadricipiti (gamba posteriore). Attiva il core e gli
obliqui durante la flessione laterale.
*Obiettivo:* Migliora la mobilità dell'anca (rotazione interna ed esterna) e allevia la tensione nella zona lombare.

en.name: YTWL Exercise
en.instructions:
Purpose:Improves shoulder stability, posture, and scapular (shoulder blade) control. Often used in physical therapy and warm-ups.
*Starting Position:
Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Hinge forward at the hips (like a
deadlift) keeping your back flat, or lie face down on an incline bench.
Keep your thumbs pointing up throughout.
*Y (Arms up):
Extend both arms straight forward and upward at a 135-degree angle from
your body, forming a "Y". Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the
top.
*T (Arms out):Open your arms straight out to the sides, perpendicular to your body, forming a "T". Focus on pinching your shoulder blades.
*W (Arms bent):Pull your elbows back, bending them to 90 degrees, and squeeze your shoulder blades to form a "W". Keep your wrists firm.
*L (Arms rotated):
Start with elbows bent at 90 degrees and close to your body. Rotate
your forearms outward (external rotation) like a goalpost, forming an
"L" or a gate.
*Key Focus:*
Movements should be slow and controlled. Always lead with the thumbs
and think about moving the shoulder blades, not just the arms.

it.name: Esercizio YTWL
it.instructions:
Obiettivo:
Migliorare la stabilità della spalla, la postura e il controllo delle
scapole. Ampiamente usato in fisioterapia e nel riscaldamento.
*Posizione iniziale:
In piedi con i piedi alla larghezza delle spalle. Piega il busto in
avanti mantenendo la schiena dritta (come uno stacco), oppure sdraiati a
pancia in giù su una panca inclinata. Tieni i pollici sempre rivolti
verso l'alto.
*Y (Braccia in alto):
Distendi entrambe le braccia dritte in avanti e verso l'alto con un
angolo di 135° rispetto al corpo, formando una "Y". Unisci le scapole
nel punto più alto.
*T (Braccia aperte):Apri le braccia lateralmente, perpendicolari al corpo, formando una "T". Concentrati sullo stringere le scapole.
*W (Braccia piegate):Tira i gomiti indietro piegandoli a 90°, stringendo le scapole per formare una "W". Tieni i polsi fermi.
*L (Rotazione esterna):
Gomiti piegati a 90° e vicini al corpo. Ruota gli avambracci verso
l'esterno (rotazione esterna) come dei pali della porta, formando una
"L".
*Attenzione:*
I movimenti devono essere lenti e controllati. Guida sempre il
movimento con i pollici e concentrati sul movimento delle scapole, non
solo delle braccia.

en.name: Supine Hip Abduction
en.instructions:
Starting Position:
Lie on your back (supine) on a mat, with your legs extended and
relaxed. Arms can be placed alongside your body or out to the sides for
stability.
*The Movement:
Slightly lift one leg off the floor (keeping it straight or with a
slight bend). Move it laterally outward, away from the other leg, as if
stepping over a small obstacle.
*Range of Motion:
Move the leg as far as comfortable without lifting your pelvis or
rotating your torso, feeling a stretch in the inner thigh and hip.
*Return:Slowly bring the leg back to the starting position with controlled movement.
*Goal:* Improves lateral hip mobility (abduction) and strengthens the pelvic stabilizer muscles.

it.name: Abduzione dell'anca in posizione supina
it.instructions:
Posizione iniziale:
Sdraiati sulla schiena (supini) su un tappetino, con le gambe distese e
rilassate. Le braccia possono essere lungo i fianchi o aperte per
maggiore stabilità.
*Il movimento:
Solleva leggermente una gamba da terra (mantenendola tesa o con una
leggera flessione). Spostala lateralmente verso l'esterno,
allontanandola dall'altra gamba, come se dovessi scavalcare un piccolo
ostacolo.
*Ampiezza:
Porta la gamba più in là possibile senza sollevare il bacino o ruotare
il busto, sentendo un allungamento nella parte interna della coscia e
dell'anca.
*Ritorno:Riporta lentamente la gamba alla posizione iniziale, controllando il movimento.
*Obiettivo:* Migliora la mobilità laterale dell'anca (abduzione) e allena i muscoli stabilizzatori del bacino.

en.name: Decline Bench Leg Raise
en.instructions:
• *Setup: Lie on a decline bench with your head at the top and grip the handles.
• The Start: Extend legs fully, keeping them slightly elevated to engage your core.
• The Lift: Raise your legs toward the ceiling using your abs, not momentum.
• The Squeeze: Pause and contract your lower abdominals at the top.
• The Return*: Lower your legs slowly to the starting position with control.

en.name: Overhead Barbell Press
en.instructions:
• *Setup:Stand with feet together and grip the bar slightly wider than shoulders.
• Position:Rest the bar on your upper chest.
• Press:Brace your core and push the bar straight up until your arms lock out.
• Finish:* Control the bar back down to your chest.
• https://youtu.be/ZXpdJOLNoWw?si=u27cGyODoblXHBu1

en.name: Tricep Rope Pushdowns
en.instructions:
• *Setup:Stand facing the cable, feet shoulder-width apart, with a slight forward lean.
• Grip:Hold the rope with palms facing each other and elbows tucked tight to your ribs.
• Execution:Push the rope down until arms are fully straight, pulling the ends apart at the bottom.
• Control:* Keep upper arms still and return to the start with a slow, controlled motion.

en.name: Clean and Press
en.instructions:
The First Pull:Lift the bar from the floor to knee-height by driving with the legs, keeping the angle of your back constant.
*The "Power" Position:As the bar reaches mid-thigh, explosively shrug and extend your hips to create vertical momentum.
*The Quick Elbow Turnover:In the catch phase, rotate your elbows rapidly under the bar to create a "shelf" on your front deltoids.
*The Vertical Press:* Press the bar in a straight line; your head should shift slightly forward once the bar clears your forehead to reach full lockout.

en.name: Weighted push-ups
en.instructions:
• *Setup:Begin in a standard plank position with a weight plate balanced securely on your upper back.
• Alignment:Maintain a straight line from your head to your heels, engaging your core to prevent your back from sagging.
• Execution:Lower your body until your chest nearly touches the floor, keeping your elbows at a forty-five degrees.
• Ascent:* Press through your palms to return to the starting position, fully extending your arms.

en.instructions: Set weight and grip for the cables in the cage. Take a few steps away, bend over, pull and extend the back at the same time.

en.name: Hip Bridge
en.instructions:

en.name: Unilateral Lunges

en.name: Butterfly Superman

en.name: Leg Wheel
en.instructions:
Lay on the back and lift legs in perpendicular fashion, keeping the knees together.

Start making small circles in one direction with both of your knees with very small range of motion, focusing on abs and keeping your back in contact with the floor.

en.name: Kneeling Superman
en.instructions:
• Push one foot back until leg fully extended, concentrating on the having the foot high and pushed back as if pulled.

• Extend arm forward with focus having the shoulder high up.

Unilateral and static hold.

en.name: Cat Plank
en.instructions:
On your fours and raise the knees of the floor ever so slightly. 
Curl your back out and push back from your shoulders as to resemble a cat making itself look large.

en.name: Core Rotation
en.instructions: Sit back, raise feet above the ground with knees bent and start rotating left and right with hands touching the ground every move.

en.name: Unilateral Hip Thrust
en.instructions: Extend one leg while laying down and start raising your body with one leg touching the ground through the heel.

en.name: Isometria alle parallele
en.instructions: The parallel bars isometric hold is a static upper-body exercise performed on dip bars (parallel bars). Instead of moving up and down like in a traditional dip, you hold a fixed position under tension.

en.name: Quadruped Hip Abduction
en.instructions:
Distribute your body weight evenly on all knees and arms.
Keep the torso stable, with the abdomen engaged and the lumbar spine
straight without twisting the back (imagine: a glass on your lower back
won't fall off). Raise one leg outwards without twisting it.

Pay attention to the right angle at the hips and knees. Always train both sides of the body.

To increase resistance, a resistance band can be used.

en.instructions: Deep loaded stretch for pectorals, typically performed at end of chest work.

en.name: Extreme Shoulder Stretch
en.instructions: Deep loaded stretch for deltoids, performed after pressing movements.

en.name: Extreme Lat Stretch
en.instructions: Deep loaded stretch for latissimus dorsi, performed after pulling movements.

en.name: Seated Cable chest fly
en.instructions:
1. Place a bench between two cable pulleys and adjust the pulleys so they are at chest/shoulder height when you are seated.
2. Grab the handles with a neutral grip and lean against the upright backrest.
3. Bring your arms together in front of your chest in a controlled motion, focusing on squeezing your chest muscles. Keep your elbows slightly bent throughout the movement.
4. Pause briefly at the top position.
5. Slowly lower your arms back to the starting position while maintaining control of the movement.
6. Repeat for reps.

en.name: Barbell Silverback Shrug
en.instructions:
1. Stand with your feet shoulder width apart holding the barbell with both hands in front just past shoulder width.
2. Bend forward at the hips with a slight bend in your knees, keeping your back straight.
3. Engage your shoulder blades, as if you are trying to touch them together.
4. Release the shrug.
Description taken from MuscleWiki

en.name: Inverted Lat Pull Down
en.instructions: The *Inverted Lat Pull Down(most commonly known as the Reverse Grip Lat Pull Down) is a variation of the standard exercise that uses an underhand (supinated) grip with hands at shoulder-width. This position shifts more emphasis to the lower latsand increases biceps* involvement, often allowing for a greater range of motion and a deeper squeeze at the bottom of the movement.

en.name: Seated V-Grip Row
en.instructions: The *Seated V-Grip Rowis a compound pulling exercise performed on a cable machine using a close-grip "V" handle. While seated with your feet braced, you pull the handle toward your midsection, focusing on back thickness* and mid-back development.

en.name: Assisted Pull-Up
en.instructions: The *Assisted Pull-Up* is a compound vertical pulling exercise performed on a machine with a counterweight platform or by using resistance bands. It mimics the mechanics of a standard pull-up but reduces the total weight you have to lift, making it an excellent tool for building functional strength and perfecting your technique.

en.name: Dumbbell Curl
en.instructions: The *Dumbbell Curl* is a classic isolation exercise for the arms. Unlike the Hammer Curl, it involves rotating your wrists (supination) as you lift the weights, which allows for a full contraction of the biceps.

en.name: Abdominal Crunch
en.instructions: The *Abdominal Crunch* is a classic core isolation exercise performed on the floor or a mat. Unlike a full sit-up, it involves a smaller range of motion where you only lift your shoulders and upper back off the ground, keeping your lower back pressed firmly against the floor.

en.name: Belt Squat
en.instructions: Belt Squat: a squat variation done with a belt attached to a loading machine or platform so the weight is supported at the hips instead of on the spine. It mainly trains the quads and glutes, with much less lower-back fatigue than a barbell squat. Use a full range of motion, keep the torso upright, and drive through the mid-foot.

en.name: Cable Rear-Delt Fly (single arm)
en.instructions:
*Cable rear delt fly (single arm):
Stand sideways to a cable machine with the handle set around shoulder height. With a slight bend in the elbow, pull the handle out and back in a wide arc so the upper arm moves away from the body. Keep your torso still and focus on the rear delt doing the work. Use light to moderate weight* and controlled reps.

en.name: Cat-Cow
en.instructions: On all fours. Arch spine up (cat) then drop it down (cow). Breathe with movement.

en.name: Neck CARs
en.instructions: Controlled Articular Rotations. Slow full circles 3 each way. Cervical mobility.

en.name: Diaphragmatic Breathing
en.instructions: Belly breathing. Hand on chest stays still, hand on belly rises. 8-10 slow breaths.

en.name: dumbbell snatch
en.instructions:
Key Steps to Execute Correctly:

Setup: Place the dumbbell between your feet, with your shoulders above your hips, chest up, and back flat.

The Pull: Explosively extend your hips, knees, and ankles (triple extension) to drive the dumbbell upward, keeping your elbow high and the dumbbell close to your body.

The Catch: Quickly flex your hips and knees to drop under the dumbbell and receive it overhead with your arm locked in position, landing in a half-squat stance.

Common Mistakes: Using your arms too much to lift the weight instead of your legs, having a low elbow during the pull phase, and misaligning your shoulder, elbow, and wrist in the final position. For beginners, it’s recommended to start with light loads, focus on technique, and perform 3 to 5 sets of 3 to 5 reps per arm.

en.name: 1 Leg Box Squat
en.instructions: This exercise requires a sturdy box or a chair. Simple stand ~6 inches in front of it and balance yourself on one leg. From here, begin squatting down in a smooth controlled motion while keeping your other leg straight out in front of you for balance. Slowly sit down on the box, pause for a 1 count and push back up with the working leg, while never letting your other leg touch the ground.

en.name: Step Jack
en.instructions:
The Step Jack is a low-impact plyometric-style move that provides cardiovascular benefits without the joint stress of jumping. It works the entire body, specifically targeting the legs, core, and shoulders. This move is ideal for beginners, individuals with joint sensitivities, or as a dynamic warm-up to gradually elevate the heart rate.
Notes (Instructions):
1. ​Stand upright with your feet together and arms at your sides.
2. ​Step your right foot out to the side while simultaneously swinging both arms up above your head.
3. Bring your right foot back to the center and lower your arms.
4. ​Immediately repeat the movement, stepping out with your left foot.
5. ​Continue alternating sides at a steady, rhythmic pace.

en.name: Slow Squat
en.instructions:
​A tempo-based squat that uses controlled movement to increase muscle tension and improve lower-body stability.
1. ​Lower: Descend slowly for 3 seconds.
2. ​Pause: Hold at the bottom for 1 second.
3. ​Stand: Return to the starting position at a normal pace.
4. Form: Keep your chest up and weight in your heels.

en.name: Wide Push-Up
en.instructions:
​A push-up variation with a wider hand placement to increase the emphasis on the outer chest muscles and shoulders.
1. ​Setup: Place hands wider than shoulder-width apart on the floor.
1. Lower: Descend until your chest nearly touches the floor, keeping your core tight.
1. ​Push: Drive through your palms to return to the start position.
1. ​Form: Don't let your lower back sag; keep a straight line from head to heels.

en.name: Marching High Knees
en.instructions:
A low-impact cardio and mobility exercise that strengthens the hip flexors and improves balance.
1. ​Movement: Stand tall and lift one knee toward your chest as high as comfortable.
1. ​Arms: Swing the opposite arm forward as you lift your knee, similar to a walking motion.
1. ​Core: Keep your abs engaged to maintain an upright posture.
1. ​Pace: Perform the movement with control, alternating legs rhythmically.

en.name: 1/2 Kneeling Thoracic Rotation
en.instructions:
• Begin in a half kneeling position with the
leg away from the wall stabilized against the wall
with a ball.
• With both hands directly in front of
you, rotate one arm open attempting to reach
the wall behind you.
• Exhale as you rotate, inhale
as you return to neutral and repeat.

Note: You will feel the mid-back and shoulder open with this exercise.
Note: Avoid rotating from your lower back. The motion should primarily be occurring in your mid-back

en.name: lento avanti seduto
en.instructions: slow controlled seated forward exercise with dumbbells

en.name: Single-arm dumbbell shoulder press
en.instructions:
Press the dumbbell vertically overhead in a controlled motion until your arm is fully extended, without locking the elbow. Slowly lower the dumbbell back to the starting position at shoulder height.

Note: Keep your core tight throughout the movement to avoid lateral trunk lean
Note: Do not arch your lower back as you press
Note: Keep your wrist neutral and aligned with your forearm
Note: Control the descent: do not drop the weight

en.name: Single-arm cable pushdown
en.instructions:
Single-arm cable pushdown is a unilateral isolation exercise that targets the triceps brachii. By working one arm at a time, it helps correct strength imbalances between sides while also engaging the core for stability.
Starting position:
Stand facing the cable machine with your feet shoulder-width apart. Attach a single handle to the high pulley. Grab the handle with one hand using an overhand grip (pronated), with your elbow bent at approximately 90° and tucked close to your body. Keep your core braced and your back straight.
Execution:
Push the handle downward in a controlled motion by extending your elbow until your arm is fully extended. Hold the contraction for 1 second at the bottom, then slowly return to the starting position.

Note: Keep your elbow fixed and close to your body throughout the movement
Note: Do not swing your torso or use momentum
Note: Control the return: do not let the weight pull your arm up
Note: Keep your wrist neutral and firm

en.name: Kettlebell sumo high pull
en.instructions:
A compound exercise combining elements of a sumo deadlift and a high pull. It targets the posterior chain, particularly the glutes, hamstrings, and upper back. The sumo stance increases hip engagement, while the high pull adds an explosive element, promoting power development.

Stand upright overtop of a kettlebell with your feet wider than shoulder-width apart angled out slightly.
Maintain a braced core and neutral spine throughout the exercise.
Hinge your hips backward and extend your arms to grab ahold the kettlebell with a double overhand grip.
With you lower legs nearly vertical to the ground, extend your hips to raise the kettlebell with your elbows high keeping it close to your body.
• Once the kettlebell has reached shoulder height, lower back to the starting position.

en.name: Mentzer Pulldown
en.instructions: Close grip front facing Pull down, while focusing on Biceps, Increases activation of biceps over the whole range, Avoid activating Lats.

en.name: Single-Arm Lat Pulldown
en.instructions:
Sit at the lat pulldown machine and grab the single handle with a neutral grip. Keep your torso stable, your chest lifted, and your shoulder blades slightly retracted. Start with your arm fully extended overhead, then pull the handle down toward your upper chest following a controlled, slightly diagonal path. Focus on engaging the latissimus dorsi while keeping the shoulder depressed and avoiding any torso rotation. Slowly return to the starting position, maintaining full control throughout the movement.

Note: Keep the shoulder down and away from the ear during the entire movement.
Note: Avoid leaning or twisting your torso to assist the pull.
Note: Control the eccentric phase and avoid letting the weight pull you upward.
Note: Focus on pulling with the back muscles, not with the biceps.
Note: Keep the elbow close to the body in the final part of the pull.

it.name: Lat machine monolaterale con maniglia
it.instructions:
Siediti alla lat machine e afferra la maniglia singola con una presa neutra. Mantieni il busto stabile, il petto sollevato e le scapole leggermente addotte. Inizia con il braccio completamente esteso sopra la testa, quindi tira la maniglia verso la parte alta del petto seguendo una traiettoria controllata e leggermente diagonale. Concentrati sull’attivazione del gran dorsale mantenendo la spalla depressa ed evitando qualsiasi rotazione del busto. Ritorna lentamente alla posizione iniziale mantenendo sempre il controllo del movimento.

Note: Mantieni la spalla bassa e lontana dall’orecchio per tutto il movimento.
Note: Evita di inclinare o ruotare il busto per aiutarti nella tirata.
Note: Controlla la fase eccentrica e non lasciare che il peso ti tiri verso l’alto.
Note: Concentrati nel tirare con i muscoli della schiena, non con i bicipiti.
Note: Mantieni il gomito vicino al corpo nella parte finale della tirata.

en.name: Hip Airplane
en.instructions:
Stand on one leg and lean your upper body slightly forward while keeping your back straight. Extend the free leg behind you so that your torso and leg form roughly one line. Slowly open your hip to the side by rotating your pelvis and upper body in a controlled way. Then close the hip again and return to the starting position.

The movement should mainly come from the hip. Keep your standing foot stable and avoid letting your knee collapse inward.

en.name: Reverse Clamshell
en.instructions:
Lie on your side with your hips and knees bent, keeping your knees stacked on top of each other. Keep your feet together at first, then keep your knees touching while lifting your top foot upward. Slowly lower the foot back down with control.

Move only through the hip and avoid rolling your pelvis backward. The movement should be small, controlled, and focused on hip rotation.

en.name: Clamshell to Reverse Clamshell
en.instructions:
Lie on your side with your hips and knees bent, keeping your legs stacked. Lift your top knee into a clamshell position and keep the leg elevated throughout the movement. From there, alternate between opening the knee upward and lifting the foot upward, moving through hip external and internal rotation.

Keep the movement slow and controlled. Do not let the top leg rest on the bottom leg between repetitions.

en.name: Curl De Muñeca Con Barra
en.instructions:
This is a variation of the flat bench press designed to emphasize the clavicular head of the pectoralis major (the upper portion). By tilting the torso, the angle of the push changes, shifting more tension to the upper chest and shoulders, which helps achieve a more aesthetic, balanced, and three-dimensional development of the torso.

1. Starting Position: Grip a bar with an overhand grip (palms facing up) at a width similar to your shoulders.

2. Position on the Bench: Kneel in front of a flat bench and rest the backs of your forearms on it. Your wrists and hands should extend slightly beyond the edge of the bench to allow for a full range of motion.

3. Eccentric Phase (Lowering): Lower the bar in a controlled manner by extending your wrists toward the floor. At the bottom of the movement, slightly spread your fingers to let the bar roll down a bit, maximizing the stretch.

4. Concentric Phase (Lift): First, close your fingers to secure the bar, then flex your wrists upward explosively but in a controlled manner, bringing the bar as high as possible. Strongly contract your forearms at the top position for one second.

5. Form: Keep your forearms firmly pressed against the bench throughout the exercise; only your wrists and fingers should move.

en.name: YTW Raises
en.instructions:
The YTW exercise for scapular retraction is designed to strengthen the inter-scapular muscles between your shoulder blades, to help retract or pull your shoulders back, helping to maintain proper upright posture.

Note: Start in neutral standing posture.
Note: Bring your arms up to roughly 135 degrees for the Y position, slightly in front of you, then bring your arms backwards by squeezing your shoulder blades together.
Note: Concentrate on squeezing the shoulder blade or scapula contraction at the end range of motion, holding this position for 3-5 seconds. Then release.
Note: Bring your arms down to roughly 90 degrees, rotate your thumbs outwards, and bring your arms backwards by squeezing your shoulder blades again with scapular retraction.
Note: For the W component, keep your arms around 90 degrees, but bring them backwards in a slight W position
Note: squeezing at the end range-focusing on the middle and lower inter-scapular fibers.

en.name: Glute-Ham Raise
en.instructions: Kneel on a glute-ham developer or have a partner hold your ankles. Keeping hips straight, lower your torso toward the floor under control, then curl back up by contracting the hamstrings and glutes.

en.name: Easy Continuous Swim (Freestyle)
en.instructions: Swim freestyle at a relaxed, steady pace without stopping: think conversation pace, not racing. Focus on smooth, even strokes rather than speed or breathing technique; this is just to get your body moving and your heart rate up.

en.name: Kick with Board
en.instructions: Hold a kickboard with both hands, arms extended in front of you, face in the water (lift head forward to breathe when needed). Kick from your hips, not your knees, keeping your legs mostly straight with a slight bend and a steady, compact flutter kick. This builds leg endurance and keeps your body horizontal without needing to worry about your arms.

en.name: Bobbing Exhale Drill
en.instructions: Stand in chest-deep water. Take a breath, submerge your face fully, and exhale slowly and completely through your nose and/or mouth the whole time you're underwater: a gentle humming sound can help keep the exhale steady and controlled. Once you're empty of air, lift your head, take a fresh breath, and go back under. Repeat continuously. The goal is training your body that all your exhaling happens underwater, so all you need to do at the surface is inhale.

en.name: Wall-Hold Rotation
en.instructions: Hold the pool wall or edge with one hand, body horizontal at the surface, legs kicking gently behind you. Keep your face in the water, exhaling continuously, then rotate your head to the side: not lifting it up: so one goggle stays in the water while the other clears the surface. Take a quick breath, then rotate your face back down to neutral. This isolates the head-rotation motion without any arm strokes to think about.

en.name: Side-Kick Breathing (Kickboard)
en.instructions: Push off the wall on your side (not flat on your stomach), one arm extended forward holding the board or just extended, kicking continuously. Keep your head in a neutral position looking at the bottom of the pool, and when you need air, rotate your head sideways (one ear stays in the water, other faces up) to breathe, then rotate back to neutral. Swim a length like this, then repeat on the other side. This teaches the exact head position and rotation you'll use once full stroke breathing comes in.

en.name: Stroke-and-Roll Drill
en.instructions: Push off, swim a few strokes, and every breath roll fully onto your back for 2-3 breaths, then roll back into freestyle. This teaches you to rotate your body as a unit rather than just turning your head, and helps remove the fear of not having your face in the water.

en.name: Recovery Bobbing
en.instructions: Same motion as the Bobbing Exhale Drill, but done in slightly deeper water (so you're not touching the bottom) and at a slower, more relaxed pace: think of it as a recovery/reset exercise rather than a hard drill. Use it between harder drills to reset your breathing rhythm and calm down if you're feeling rushed or out of sync.

en.name: Cool-Down Swim
en.instructions: Swim at an easy, unhurried pace: freestyle, backstroke, or just floating/gliding: with zero focus on technique or drills. The only goal here is to let your heart rate come down gradually and your muscles relax before you get out of the pool.

en.name: Posterior Pelvic Tilt
en.instructions: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat on the floor. Flatten your lower back against the floor by tilting your pelvis posteriorly, engaging your abs and glutes. Hold 5 seconds, release. This retrains pelvic positioning to counter anterior pelvic tilt.

en.name: Band Terminal Knee extension
en.instructions: This is an end range strengthening exercise for the knee extensors. Start by looping a band around the back of one knee and anchoring the other end to a stable surface in front of you. Stand in a split stance with the banded knee bent and placed as the front leg. Straighten the knee to pull against the bands resistance and maintain a contraction in your quadriceps for up to 5 seconds before releasing.

en.name: Serratus Wall Slide Stretch
en.instructions:
1. Stand facing a wall. Place your forearms vertically against the wall so your elbows and wrists are both touching it.
2. Point your arms slightly outwards from "straight up".
3. Protract your shoulders had, then slide your forearms up the wall until your elbows are about level with your chin.
4. Slide your forearms back down the wall. Repeat as necessary.

Note: Keep a hollow body position; don't allow your back to arch.
Note: Keep your shoulders protracted through the movement.

en.name: Couch Stretch
en.instructions:
1. Stand facing away from a bench, couch or similar-height object.
2. Extend one leg backwards, resting your foot "laces-down" on the edge of the bench.
3. Lower yourself until your rear knee is on the floor and you are in a lunge position, with your torso hanging forwards slightly.
4. Brace your core, tense your rear glute, and straighten up your torso to vertical, under control. Relax and repeat.

Repeat for the other leg, too.

en.name: Long Lunge Pulse Stretch
en.instructions:
1. Hold the resistance band (or any other rope-like object, the elasticity is not necessary) above your head, between your hands, with your arms straight. Pull it taught to engage your lats.
2. Step forwards into a lunge, dropping until your knee is almost touching the floor.
3. Slowly and controlledly pulse your body up and down by about an inch. Repeat for required reps.
4. Repeat for other leg.

en.name: Front Split Stretch
en.instructions:
1. Start kneeling.
2. Extend one leg out forwards, fully straightened. Follow with your hips so your back leg begins to unfold.
3. Carefully lower yourself into the stretch. Do not go beyond your limit.
4. Hold for the required time.

Note: Keep your body upright and straight throughout.
Note: Keep your hips square throughout.

en.name: Squat Sky Reach Stretch
en.instructions:
1. Drop into a squat.
2. Hold one ankle with the opposite hand.
3. Fold your other arm to your chest.
4. Staying in the squat and keeping hold of your ankle, twist to turn your chest-hand back/outwards until your elbow is pointing at the sky.
5. Return to the neutral squatting position with your hand on your chest. Repeat movement as required.

Repeat on both sides.

Note: If you can, at the top of the stretch uncoil your arm and reach your hand for the sky, returning your hand to your chest on the way down.

en.name: explosive push ups
en.instructions:
Explosive Push-Ups

Start in a standard push-up position, lower your chest, then explosively push off the ground so your hands leave the floor. Land softly and immediately repeat.

en.name: Russian Push Ups
en.instructions:
Russian Push-Ups

Start in a standard push-up position with your hands slightly wider than shoulder-width apart. Lower your chest toward the floor, then shift your body forward while keeping your chest close to the ground. Extend your arms to return to the starting position, then reverse the movement smoothly. Keep your core tight and maintain controlled movement throughout the exercise.

en.name: elbow lever
en.instructions: ​A calisthenics static balance skill where the entire body is held straight and parallel to the ground, supported by tucking the elbows firmly into the abdomen or pelvic bones.

en.name: Planche Lean Hold
en.instructions: A straight-arm calisthenics static hold where you assume a plank position and lean the shoulders as far forward as possible past the wrists with protracted scapulae and a hollow body.

en.name: Arch Hang
en.instructions:

• Hold it for time/reps
• Start at an active hang: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HoE-C85ZlCE

en.name: Leg Extension Isometric
en.instructions: An isometric leg extension is a strengthening exercise where you contract your quadriceps muscles against an immovable resistance without changing the length of the muscle or moving your knee joint.

en.name: Bench Press Isometric
en.instructions: A bench press isometric hold is a static strength exercise where you pause and hold a barbell or dumbbells either at your chest, mid-press, or at lockout without moving for a set time

en.name: Overhead Press Isometric
en.instructions: An isometric overhead press involves holding a weight statically overhead or pushing against an immovable object at a specific point in the press without moving the joint.

en.name: Lateral Raise Isometric
en.instructions: An isometric lateral raise is a shoulder exercise where you hold your arms out to the sides at waist height for a set amount of time instead of moving up and down

en.name: Preacher Curl Isometric
en.instructions: An isometric preacher curl is a static strength exercise where you hold a fixed position on a preacher pad or and inclined bench under tension without moving the joint.

en.name: Lat Pulldown Isometric
en.instructions: An isometric Lat pulldown is a strength-building exercise where you pull the bar down to your chest and hold the contracted position at the bottom without moving your limbs for a set number of seconds

en.name: Triceps Pushdown Isometric
en.instructions: A single-arm isometric or isolated triceps pushdown is an isolation cable exercise where you pin your upper arm against your torso, hinge at the hips, and extend the elbow to achieve a peak contraction in the triceps muscle.

en.name: Boxing
en.instructions: Bag workout for boxing skill development and cardio improvement

en.name: Wrist circles
en.instructions:
Wrist circles is warm-up exercise, where you rotate your wrists in a circular motion. They improve mobility and are recommended before exercises such as pull ups, hand stands and other exercises that put pressure on your wrists.

Note: Rotate one time in both directions per rep

en.name: Retro Treadmill Walking
en.instructions: Controlled treadmill walking performed backward. Begin around 30 minutes at a controlled speed and approximately 2 to 3 percent incline if tolerated. Progress duration gradually as knee, hip, and back tolerance improves.

en.name: Kegel Exercise
en.instructions:
Lie on your back with your knees bent, or sit upright in a chair. Locate the pelvic floor muscles: they are the muscles you would use to stop the flow of urine or to hold back gas. Keep your abdomen, glutes and thighs relaxed and breathe normally throughout.

Tighten the pelvic floor muscles and lift them gently upwards and inwards. Hold the contraction for a few seconds, then release completely and rest for at least as long as you held. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.

The exercise can be varied by holding longer with a light contraction (endurance) or by performing quick, short contractions with a full relaxation in between.

en.name: Supported Split Squat
en.instructions: Supported split squat performed with stable balance support and controlled depth.

en.name: 90/90 Breathing
en.instructions: Controlled breathing drill performed in a 90/90 position to encourage rib, abdominal, and pelvic coordination.

en.name: 90/90 Hip Switches
en.instructions:
Sit on the floor with one leg bent at 90 degrees in front of you and the other leg bent at 90 degrees out to the side, so that the rear shin is parallel to the front shin. Keep your torso upright and, if possible, your hands off the floor.

Rotate both knees over to the other side so that the legs swap positions and you arrive in the same 90/90 position facing the opposite way. Move slowly and under control, keeping the feet in contact with the floor, and alternate sides for the desired number of repetitions.

Mobility drill for internal and external rotation of the hips.

en.name: Adductor Rock Backs
en.instructions:
Start on all fours with your hands under your shoulders and your knees under your hips. Extend one leg straight out to the side with the foot flat on the floor and the toes pointing forward.

Keep your back flat and slowly push your hips back towards the heel of the kneeling leg until you feel a stretch along the inside of the extended leg. Pause briefly, then return to the starting position. Complete all repetitions on one side before switching legs.

Mobility exercise for the adductors and the hips.

en.name: Elevated Hamstring Stretch
en.instructions:
Stand facing a bar, box or bench at roughly hip height and place the heel of one leg on it. Keep that leg straight with the toes pointing up, and keep the standing leg straight with both hips square to the support.

Hinge forward at the hips with a flat back until you feel a stretch in the back of the elevated thigh. Hold the position while breathing calmly, then switch legs.

Stretch for the hamstrings. The height of the support controls the intensity: the higher the leg, the stronger the stretch.

en.name: Single-leg BOSU balance
en.instructions:
# Single-Leg BOSU Balance Exercise

The exercise for balancing on a BOSU ball while standing on one leg is known as the single-leg BOSU balance exercise. This exercise is effective for enhancing balance, coordination, and core stability.

## Benefits of the Single-Leg BOSU Balance Exercise
Improves Balance:Standing on one leg challenges your stability.
*Enhances Coordination:Engaging different muscle groups helps improve overall coordination.
*Strengthens Core:The exercise activates core muscles, promoting better posture and stability.

## How to Perform the Single-Leg BOSU Balance Exercise
1. Positioning:Stand on the dome side of the BOSU ball with one leg.
2. Balance:Keep your opposite leg lifted and your core engaged.
3. Duration:Aim to hold the position for 10-20 seconds, gradually increasing the time as you improve.

## Progression Tips
*Add Movement:Try reaching for objects around you while maintaining balance.
*Close Your Eyes:This increases the challenge by removing visual stability cues.
*Use a Ball:* Catch or toss a ball while balancing to further engage your core and coordination.

This exercise is a great way to build foundational balance skills before progressing to more complex movements.

en.name: Quad Sets
en.instructions:
# What Are Quad Sets?

Quad sets are a fundamental exercise used in knee rehabilitation. They focus on strengthening the quadriceps muscles located at the front of the thigh. This exercise is particularly beneficial for individuals recovering from knee injuries or surgeries.

## How to Perform Quad Sets

### Steps to Execute Quad Sets

1. *Positioning:Sit or lie down with your legs straight.
2. Tightening:Tighten the quadriceps muscles while keeping the leg straight. You should see the kneecap move upward.
3. Holding:Maintain the contraction for about 5 seconds.
4. Releasing:Relax the muscle after the hold.
5. Repetitions:Aim for 10 to 15 repetitions, gradually increasing as strength improves.

### Tips for Effective Quad Sets

• Ensure no other muscles are contracting to assist the quadriceps.
• Perform the exercise on a flat surface, like a bed or couch, with a towel or pillow under your heel for comfort.
• It is recommended to do these exercises multiple times a day, especially during the early stages of recovery.

## Benefits of Quad Sets

• Restores Muscle Function:Helps rebuild strength in the quadriceps.
• Improves Stability:Enhances stability in the knee joint.
• Increases Range of Motion:* Aids in regaining mobility after injury or surgery.

Incorporating quad sets into your rehabilitation routine can significantly aid in recovery and improve overall knee function.

en.name: Hip-Out and Hip-In Lateral Steps
en.instructions:
# Overview of Hip-Out and Hip-In Lateral Steps

Hip-out and hip-in lateral steps are effective exercises designed to strengthen the hip abductors and enhance lateral stability. These movements are beneficial for improving coordination and overall hip function.

## Exercise Descriptions

### Hip-Out Steps

• *Movement:Step out to the side with one leg, keeping the other leg stable.
• Target Muscles:Primarily engages the hip abductors, including the gluteus medius and minimus.
• Benefits:Increases lateral stability and strength in the hip area.

### Hip-In Steps

• Movement:Bring the leg back in toward the center after stepping out.
• Target Muscles:Continues to engage the hip abductors while also activating the adductors.
• Benefits:Enhances coordination and control of the hip joint.

## Key Benefits of Lateral Steps

| Benefit | Description |
|---|---|
| Strengthening Hip Abductors| Improves muscle strength around the hip joint. |
| Enhancing Stability| Increases lateral stability, reducing the risk of falls. |
| Improving Coordination* | Develops better control and movement patterns in the hips. |

Incorporating hip-out and hip-in lateral steps into a regular exercise routine can lead to improved hip strength and stability, which is essential for various physical activities and daily movements.

en.name: Single-Leg Soft-Landing Holds
en.instructions:
# Single-Leg Soft-Landing Holds

Single-leg soft-landing holds are exercises that focus on balance and stability by landing softly on one leg and holding the position. This exercise helps improve proprioception and can be beneficial for rehabilitation and athletic training.

## Overview

Single-leg soft-landing holds are exercises designed to enhance balance, stability, and proprioception. They involve landing softly on one leg and maintaining that position for a brief period. This exercise is particularly useful in rehabilitation settings and for athletes looking to improve their performance.

## Benefits

• *Improves balance:Enhances stability by training the body to control weight distribution on one leg.
• Enhances proprioception:Increases awareness of body position, which is crucial for injury prevention.
• Supports rehabilitation:Helps individuals recover from lower-limb injuries by strengthening muscles and improving joint stability.

## How to Perform Single-Leg Soft-Landing Holds

### Steps

1. Preparation:Stand on a stable surface or a box.
2. Takeoff:Step off the box or surface with one leg, ensuring that you do not jump.
3. Landing:Land softly on the target leg, allowing the knee and hip to bend slightly.
4. Hold position:Maintain balance in the landed position for up to 2 seconds.
5. Reset:* Return to the starting position and repeat.

### Key Points to Remember

• Keep your chest up and engage your core for better stability.
• Ensure your knee aligns with the midline of your foot during landing.
• Focus on a controlled descent to minimize impact.

## Conclusion

Incorporating single-leg soft-landing holds into your training routine can significantly enhance your balance and stability, making it a valuable exercise for both rehabilitation and athletic performance.

en.name: Reverse V-Squat
en.instructions:
Step into the V-squat machine facing the pad, the opposite way from the regular V-squat, so that your chest rests against the pad and your shoulders sit under the shoulder pads. Place your feet on the platform about shoulder width apart and release the safety.

Brace your core and lower yourself by bending your knees and pushing the hips back until your thighs are roughly parallel to the platform. Drive back up through the heels without locking out the knees.

Compared to the regular V-squat, the reversed position shifts the emphasis towards the glutes and hamstrings.

en.name: Banded Front Raise
en.instructions:
Stand on the middle of a resistance band with feet about hip-width apart, holding one end in each hand in front of your thighs. Keeping your arms straight with a slight bend in the elbows, raise your hands forward to shoulder height, then lower slowly under control. Can be done with both arms together or alternating. Use a heavier band or shorten the band to increase resistance.

Note: Stand on more of the band to increase resistance. Note: Lower under control instead of letting the band snap back. Note: Keep a slight, fixed bend in the elbows throughout. Note: Stop at shoulder height; going higher shifts the work to the traps.

en.name: Plate-Loaded Lat Pulldown
en.instructions:
Sit at a plate-loaded (lever) lat pulldown machine with your thighs secured under the pads. Grip the handles overhead with arms fully extended. Pull the handles down toward your upper chest by driving your elbows down and back, squeezing your lats at the bottom. Return slowly to full extension. Resistance comes from weight plates loaded on the machine's lever arms rather than a cable stack.

Note: Keep the torso near vertical; leaning back turns it into a row. Note: Let the arms extend fully at the top of each rep. Note: Set the seat so the handles start above your head with arms fully extended. Note: Drive the elbows down and back rather than pulling with the hands.

en.name: Lean-Away Cable Lateral Raise
en.instructions:
Set a cable pulley at the lowest position and attach a single handle. Stand side-on to the machine, hold the frame with your near hand and lean your body away so you hang at an angle. With the far hand, grasp the handle in front of your hips and raise your arm out to the side to shoulder height with a slight bend in the elbow. Lower slowly. The lean increases tension on the side delts at the bottom of the movement. Complete all reps, then switch sides.

Note: Raise to shoulder height, no higher. Note: The lean is what keeps tension on the side delt at the bottom. Note: Hold the frame firmly and let your body hang away at a steady angle. Note: Lead with the elbow, keeping a slight bend in it.

en.name: Seated Band Row
en.instructions:
Sit on the floor with your legs straight out in front of you and your back tall. Loop a resistance band around the soles of both feet and hold one end in each hand, arms extended and a slight bend in the knees. Pull the band toward your lower ribs by driving your elbows straight back and squeezing your shoulder blades together. Keep your chest up and your torso still rather than rocking backward to move the band. Extend the arms slowly to return. Because the torso stays upright and supported, this is a useful row when a bent-over position is uncomfortable, and it needs no anchor point.

Note: Keep the torso still; don't rock backward to finish the rep. Note: Shorten your grip on the band for more resistance. Note: Sit tall: hips stacked under the shoulders, chest up. Note: Pull to the lower ribs, not the chest.

en.name: FlexBar Wrist Extension
en.instructions:
Performed with a flexible resistance bar such as a Theraband FlexBar. Rest your forearm on your thigh or a table with the palm facing down and the wrist just past the edge. Hold the bar in that hand, let the wrist drop, then extend the wrist to raise the bar, keeping the forearm still. Lower slowly, taking about three seconds. The resistance comes from twisting or bending the flexible bar, so a thicker or stiffer bar increases the load. Commonly used for wrist and forearm strengthening and for elbow tendon rehabilitation.

Note: Use a lighter bar if you feel it in the elbow joint rather than the forearm muscles. Note: Rest the forearm on your thigh so only the wrist moves. Note: Lower over about three seconds; the slow part matters most.

en.name: FlexBar Wrist Flexion
en.instructions:
Performed with a flexible resistance bar such as a Theraband FlexBar. Rest your forearm on your thigh or a table with the palm facing up and the wrist just past the edge. Hold the bar in that hand, let the wrist extend back, then curl the wrist up to raise the bar while the forearm stays still. Lower slowly, taking about three seconds. Works the wrist flexors, and is the companion movement to FlexBar wrist extension for balanced forearm strengthening.

Note: Palm faces up; the forearm stays flat on the thigh. Note: Curl the wrist, don't lift the arm. Note: Pair with wrist extension so both sides of the forearm get worked.

en.name: FlexBar Tyler Twist
en.instructions:
An eccentric exercise for the wrist extensors, done with a flexible resistance bar such as a Theraband FlexBar, and widely used in rehabilitation for lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow). Hold the bar vertically in the affected hand with the wrist extended. Grasp the top of the bar with the other hand, palm facing away, and twist the top hand to wind up the bar. Bring both arms out in front of you with the bar horizontal, then slowly let the affected wrist untwist the bar over about four seconds while the other hand holds steady. Reset and repeat. The reverse version, twisting in the opposite direction for the wrist flexors, is used for medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow). Move slowly and stop if the exercise causes sharp pain rather than the expected mild discomfort.

Note: The working wrist does the slow unwinding; the other hand just holds position. Note: Take about four seconds to let the bar untwist. Note: Mild discomfort in the forearm is expected; sharp joint pain is not. Note: Reverse the twist direction to target the flexors for golfer's elbow.

en.name: Seated Knee Extension with Overpressure
en.instructions:
A gentle stretch to restore full knee extension. Sit with one leg stretched out in front of you and the heel propped on the floor or a low surface, so the knee is unsupported. Place both hands on the thigh just above the kneecap. Keeping the leg relaxed, gently press down through the hands toward the floor until you feel a stretch behind the knee, and hold for about three seconds before releasing. The pressure should produce a stretch, never sharp pain. Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions, then switch legs.

Note: Hold about three seconds, then release fully before the next rep. Note: Often prescribed after knee surgery or injury to restore full extension. Note: Keep the heel propped and the leg relaxed; the hands do the work. Note: Press gently toward a stretch, never into sharp pain.

en.name: Banded Monster Walk
en.instructions:
A banded walking drill for the glutes and hip stabilisers. Place a mini band around both thighs just above the knees, or around the ankles for a harder version. Stand with feet hip-width apart so the band is under tension, then sink into a quarter-squat with the chest up. Walk forward with small diagonal steps, pushing each leg out against the band and keeping the knees tracking over the toes rather than letting them fall inward. Walk forward for the prescribed number of steps, then walk backward to return, keeping the band under tension throughout.

Note: Step out and forward on a diagonal rather than straight ahead. Note: Take small, controlled steps instead of long ones. Note: Keep tension on the band the whole time; don't let the knees collapse inward. Note: Stay in a quarter-squat with the chest up.

en.name: Step Calf Stretch
en.instructions:
Stand on a step or a sturdy raised surface with the balls of both feet on the edge and the heels hanging off, holding a rail or wall for balance. Let one or both heels drop below the level of the step until you feel a stretch through the calf, and hold. Keep the knee straight to stretch the gastrocnemius, or bend the knee slightly to bias the soleus lower down. Hold for the prescribed time, typically 30 seconds, without bouncing, then switch sides if stretching one leg at a time.

Note: Bend the knee slightly to shift the stretch to the soleus. Note: Lower slowly and hold steady rather than bouncing. Note: Hold a rail or wall for balance. Note: Keep the stretching leg straight to bias the gastrocnemius.

en.name: Single-Leg Balance with Eyes Closed
en.instructions:
A balance and proprioception drill. Stand on one leg with the knee slightly bent and the other foot lifted clear of the floor, then close your eyes and hold the position. Without visual feedback the ankle and hip stabilisers have to do the work, so expect noticeable wobble. Stand within reach of a wall, counter or chair so you can steady yourself if needed. Hold for the prescribed time, then switch legs. Commonly prescribed in rehabilitation after ankle or knee injury.

Note: Keep the standing knee soft, not locked. Note: Let the foot and ankle work; small wobbles are the point. Note: Stand near a wall or counter so you can catch yourself. Note: Closing the eyes removes visual input, which is what makes this hard.

en.name: Single-Leg Balance with Kettlebell Circles
en.instructions:
A balance drill that adds a moving load. Stand on one leg with the knee slightly bent, holding a kettlebell in one hand. Pass the kettlebell around your body in a circle, handing it from one hand to the other in front and behind you, while keeping your balance on the standing leg. Keep the hips level and the torso upright; the shifting weight of the bell constantly changes your centre of mass, which is what trains the hip and ankle stabilisers. Complete the prescribed number of circles, reverse direction, then switch legs. Use a light bell to start.

Note: Move the bell smoothly, passing hand to hand behind the back. Note: Change direction halfway through the set. Note: Start light; the weight is a balance challenge, not a strength one. Note: Keep the hips level and square as the bell travels.

en.name: Bent Over Dumbbell Rows (Two Arms)
en.instructions:
*How to Perform It
• Hold a dumbbell in each hand with a neutral or overhand grip.
• Hinge at the hips, pushing your glutes back, until your torso is roughly 45-75 degrees to the floor. Keep a slight bend in your knees.
• Let the dumbbells hang directly below your shoulders with arms fully extended.
• Keep your back flat, chest up, and core braced: avoid rounding your spine.
• Pull the dumbbells up toward your ribcage/hips, driving your elbows back and squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top.
• Pause briefly at the top of the movement.
• Lower the dumbbells back down under control to the starting position.
• Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.

Key Coaching Cues*
• Hinge from the hips, not the lower back
• Keep the spine neutral throughout: no rounding
• Lead with the elbows, not the hands
• Avoid using momentum or jerking the weight up
• Control the eccentric (lowering) phase rather than letting the weights drop

en.name: Radio Taiso
en.instructions:
Video can be found here : https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGPBSqxKGAc

Full-body mobility and dynamic warm-up routine (3-5 minutes) to prepare joints, muscles, and the cardiovascular system for workout.

Movement Flow:

Deep Breathing & Arm Raises: Inhale while raising arms laterally overhead, exhale as you lower them.

Knee Bends: Soft, rhythmic knee flexions synchronized with arm swings.

Arm Circles: Large full-range arm rotations forward, then backward to open up the chest and shoulder girdle.

Chest Expansion: Cross arms in front of the chest and open wide to the sides.

Side Bends: Reach overhead to stretch the lateral torso left and right with a smooth side flexion.

Forward & Back Bends: Gently hinge at the hips to reach forward, then return upright with a mild spinal extension.

Torso Twists: Swing arms side-to-side to rotate the spine and loosen the core.

Ankle Mobility / Light Bounces: Soft heel lifts or light bouncing on toes to warm up lower leg joints and tendons.

Note: Keep movements smooth, controlled, and continuous. Do not force any range of motion.
